I first began listening to podcasts about a year and a half ago.  Chris, my former co-host, suggested The 2600 Game by Game Podcast.  I've still not caught up on all those episodes, but I'm getting close.  One of my favorite parts of any podcast, especially Ferg's podcast, are the Christmas/holiday memories that people share.  I've heard all sorts of great Atari holiday-related stories, but for some reason Ferg has been suppressing all the stories when people "boo" the Atari and are gung ho for the Bally.  It tell ya-- it's a conspiracy.  (Okay, it might be all in my head!)

I'm sure that there must be some Bally Arcade/Astrocade stories out there.  If you're one of those few people who got a Bally Arcade under the Christmas tree on Christmas Day, then I'd love to hear your story.  Maybe the Bally was your only system.  Or, perhaps you already had an Atari and you pitted the two systems against each other.  Maybe you got a Bally Arcade very early (in January 1978) before the Atari VCS was king of America's living rooms.  Or, maybe you got it as a gift while it was on clearance in 1984 for $25.  Do you have a sad tale to tell that involves asking for an Astrocade, but you got an Atari instead?  Were you were up all night crying about what might have been?  Possibly you have a four-player tale of playing 99 rounds of Checkmate against your parents and little sister on Christmas morning.

If your tale is holiday related (Christmas, Hanukkah, or whatever you celebrate), then I'd love to hear it!  Please write in (email the show) and tell us all about it.  If you're one of those awesome folks who likes to record audio feedback, then that's welcome too.

The next episode of the Astrocast will feature this holiday feedback in the December (okay, more like mid-January) episode.

I can't wait to hear your tales!

Adam

15008:
This past summer, I began going through the Arcadian newsletters to see which programs won the $100 prize in each issue.  I was pretty surprised to find out how spotty the timing of the contest was each issue.  I began making a list of all the winners, fully expecting there to be a winner every issue, but that isn't the case at all.


I wanted to flesh-out this listing more, but I probably won't get to it, so here it is for everyone to check out.  Try some of the games on this list in AstroBASIC.  Most, or maybe even all of them, are available on BallyAlley.com.


Maybe I'll make a segment on the Astrocast about the Arcadian contest; that would be neat.  Let me know if anyone is interested in such a segment.


Adam


The listing of the prizewinners follows:


Arcadian Program Prizewinners ($100 contest winners)

August 10, 2016

Compiled by Adam Trionfo



By reading through the issues of the Arcadian, I've noted that there were 17 prizewinners.  I was under the impression that there were many more than this, but there are many months when no contest took place.



March 1981     - Idea of contest announced, but no winner for this issue



April 1981     - Programming contest idea still in progress, no winner for this issue



May 1981       - $100 Arcadian Programming Contest formally announced.  Programs must be originals, not translations.  No winner this issue.



June 1981      - No winner this issue.



July 1981      - Old Bent Nose, by Bob Wiseman - ARCADIAN 3, no. 9 (Jul. 09, 1981): 96.



August 1981    - Bally Black Box, by Steve Walters - ARCADIAN 3, no. 10 (Aug. 12, 1981): 103-105.



September 1981 - Telling Time, by Bob Hensel - ARCADIAN 3, no. 11 (Sep. 11, 1981): 114-115.



October 1981   - Rebound, by Dave Martin - ARCADIAN 3, no. 12 (Oct. 05, 1981): 124. Reprint, with additions: ARCADIAN 6, no. 6 (Apr. 20, 1984): 54.



November 1981  - 4D2, by Rusty Blommaert and Dale Smith - ARCADIAN 4, no. 1 (Nov. 10, 1981): 5,8.  Reprint, for AstroBASIC: ARCADIAN 6, no. 11 (Oct. 31, 1984): 126.



December 7, 1982 - No winner this issue because there were no entries.



December 24 1982 - No winner this issue due to lack of time.



January 1982   - The Cube, by Bob Weber - ARCADIAN 4, no. 4 (Jan. 22, 1982): 36-37.



March 1982     - Budget Worksheet, by Robert Lauffer - ARCADIAN 4, no. 5 (Mar. 05, 1982): 48-50.



April 1982     - No winner this issue



May 1982       - Stranded at Rigel, Sean Walsh - ARCADIAN 4, no. 7 (May 07, 1982): 72-73.  Note: Bally BASIC only.



June 1982      - No winner this issue



July 1982      - Astro Zap 2000, by George Moses - ARCADIAN 4, no. 9 (Jul. 06, 1982): 88.



August 1982    - No winner this issue



September 1982 - No winner this issue



October 1982   - Word Hunt, by Anthony Ross - ARCADIAN 4, no. 12 (Oct. 07, 1982): 115, 117.



November 1982  - No winner this issue



December 1982  - No winner this issue



January 1983   - No winner this issue



February 1983  - No winner this issue



March 1983     - No winner this issue



April 1983     - "We have not had a contest this year yet due to a couple of technical difficulties."



May 1983       - Ghost Fleet, by Ken Lill - ARCADIAN 5, no. 7 (May 6, 1983): 107,111.



June 1983      - No Winner because there were no eligible programs.  Only reprints of the programs on the Bally Arcade tape.



July 1983      - Frog Leap, by Dave Ibach - ARCADIAN 5, no. 9 (Jul. 22, 1983): 138,146.



August 1983    - Locksmith, by Don Crider - ARCADIAN 5, no. 10 (Aug. 16, 1983): 157.



September 1983 - No winner this issue.  Possibly this is because SHUTBOX, by Joseph Spiegal, is based on a dice game that Joseph used to have when he was "younger."



October 1983   - No winner this issue.  There are actually no programs in this issue!



November 1983  - No winner this issue.  Three programs published, but they are all re-worked programs of earlier programs, not original programs.



December 1983  - Frogway, by Mike Skala - ARCADIAN 6, no. 2 (Dec. 22, 1983): 12,16.



January 1984   - No winner this issue.  GOLDDIGGER is the only published program-- and it's for Extended BASIC, so perhaps it didn't qualify for the contest.



February 1984  - Dot-to-Dot, by Joe Peoples - ARCADIAN 6, no. 4 (Feb. 23, 1984): 38.



March 1984     - No winner this issue.  Only one program published this month: GRAVITY by Fred Rodney.



April 1984     - Shoot the Duck!, by James Wilchen - ARCADIAN 6, no. 6 (Apr. 20, 1984): 58.



May 1984       - No winner this issue.  Most programs are reprints or updates.



June 1984       - Alien 2000, by Henry Sopko - ARCADIAN 6, no. 9 (Jul. 27, 1984): 74-75.



July 1984       - No winner this issue.  Four programs published this issue: two program updates (CONNECT FOUR and STATEGIC AIR COMMAND), a program based on another game (GASWELL BONANZA) and, I think, an original program called "ACME DRIVING TEST."



August 1984     - No winner this issue.  3 ARCADIAN reprints (ASTRO ZAP 2000, BASEBALL, TOWER OF HANOI), a reprint from Niagara BUGS Bulletin (CATERPILLAR), a program previously available from The Tiny Arcade on tape (QUADRON), and one game inspired by DONKEY KONG (SPACE APE).



October 1984     - No winner this issue.  This was going to be the ARCADIAN's last issue, but it came back, as a quarterly, for one more year (volume 7).  ARCADIAN reprints (BLACK BOX), 7 original programs (KONCENTRATION, CLOCK, THE GAME OF WAR, MAZE AVENGER, CRAZIE DICE, ROTATE, VIDEO:VIDEO, unnamed and uncredited program on page 114-115), 3 reprints from Niagara BUGS Bulletin (4D2, LIZZARD LUNCH and REPACK), a program previously available from WaveMakers on tape (BACKGAMMON), a program PROBABLY previously released on tape by Astrogames (METROPOLITAN ATTACK!), an update (CONNECT FOUR ENLARGED, BATTLESHIP), a possible conversion (HOCKEY), a program previously released on tape by Collins Computer Company (BALLY CHESS BOARD), a program previously released on tape by W&W Software (OTHELLO).



June 1985     - No winner this issue.



December 1985 - No winner this issue.



March 1985    - No winner this issue.



August 1985   - No winner this issue. (This is the last issue of the Arcadian)

On January 5, 2016, Lance Squire gave a list of his Astrocade projects.  I'm glad that he did, as it's good to know what's going on in the Bally community.

Lance listed several projects.  Here are my comments on them:


1) Balzerk - Lance says that completing Balzerk is partially waiting on figuring out the code for The Incredible Wizard and making the Bally talk.  I suggest that Lance tries working with David Turner on figuring out the code.  David has begun working on completing more of the disassembly of the arcade version of Wizard of Wor.  Maybe the two of them can help each other out a little bit.  Lance, have you been able to make the Bally talks at all?  How do you propose to do this?


2) Halloween Demo - Lance wants to finish his dancing Skeletons demo.  The last thing I recall about this project is that he was trying to sync the graphics better with the sound.


3) Adding Music to the Skeletons and the Christmas demo - I wasn't aware that he was working on this.  Cool!


4) Re-working Astro Battle - Lance would like to make Astro Battle work more like the Space Invaders coin-op release of the game.  I know that he had changed some of the graphics already, as well as making the missiles/bullets animated, but sometimes the animated bullets would freeze on the screen.  The cool thing about this project, is that Astro Battle is only a 4K ROM, and it wasn't even fully used.  Lance can easily double the size of the game to 8K and it will still fit comfortably on a cartridge ROM.


5) 3D Maze Display - Lance wants to take his BASIC code for a 3D maze display and

plunk it into the Basic Demo cart.  First, I don't remember ever seeing this BASIC code?  Is it done?  Is it available for download to try on real hardware?


Does anyone else have any projects brewing?

15011:
An "Eventually-Astrocade" project.  I got Keith Robinson of Intellivision Proiduciton to go on a final discussion of producing a Netrogames Intellivision.  Netrogames, as described on netrogames.com <http://netrogames.com/> is a way of turning classic games online so all games for the old system work online, assuming you’re in a 2400 km range.  The secret is beating 8ms of ping time, which can be done with Sprint Direct Connect.

I talked with Davison Inventor’s group a long time ago.   They only accept the top 1% of inventions that can potentially make money for them.   Before I was talking to Keith, a Daniel Karetski at Davison like the idea enough, where if I’m willing to pay a <$800 pre production fee and a $6k-$15k prototyping fee, which includes all the science and research to make this happen. All they ask is a small percentage to be negotiated.   Keith said it’s cheaper to produce Netrogames with this cost structure, than it would be to produce a single Intelliviiosn 2-player title to be online, and with this, ALL Games, INTV owned games, INTV Third Party games, and games for other systems who want to cooperate with us, whihc gives Intellivision productions and me an additional revenue boost.

The only reason I put an INTV related post in the Astrocade mail fourm is becuase the Astrocade would be able to benefit from this design.   With the hundreds of multiplayer games if you count Bally Basic titles could be turned online.  Besides, people are looking for new Astrocades anyway because old Astrocades are being dead due to neglect (the plush carpet of doom) , so might as well add Netrogames and have both an Astrocade you can play locally, or play online with 100% compatible Astrocade hardware. (Not truly original becuase network features are added.)

15014:
This week, for the next episode of the Astrocast podcast, Paul and I will be discussing several letters that were sent to the Arcadian.  One letter, sent August 20, 1979, is from Jeff Frederiksen, the chief engineer behind the design of the Bally Professional Arcade hardware. It seems that this letter was accompanied by some hardware. The letter simply states:

"The enclosed assemblies replace the 75361 clock driver, located in the oscillator shield. The failure of the 75361 is that the 6V high time after warm-up drops below 55ns causing the data chip to appear defective. If you do not have this sinking clock syndrome, replacement is not necessary. I hope you find the enclosed hardware description useful."

You can view the original letter here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#JeffFrederiksenLetterAugust201979


Unfortunately, this is all the information this was included in the fabrics collection. Does anybody know what Jeff is referring to here? Was this fix to the clock driver included on later releases of the Astrocade motherboard?

Adam

If you understand the schematic, it is easier. There are actually 5 different "clocks" . There are 2 that operate the DATA chip. These are labeled 7Mbar (pin 9) and 7M (pin 10). There is also a "chroma" clock that tells the system how to "sync" the colors. Then, from the DATA chip there is a "G" clock (pin 16). That goes into a flip flop circuit. This circuit produces 2 opposite pulses. When one is at 5 volts, the other is at Zero volts. Then the next time the "G" clock sends out a pulse, these switch. The 1st is then Zero and he other, 5V. These are "tuned" to turn synchronize all of the computers workings. If the timing is off, then these clocks may operate at different times, causing things to not work right.This could cause excessive heating in the chips also. That is why it seems like the DATA chip is bad when it really is not. The only way to check a DATA chip is to swap it with a chip in a working unit. If it then works...KEEP IT. you can either use it for a spare or try swapping the other custom chips 1 at a time, If one make the good unit stop working... TURN IT OFF IMMEDIATELY. Throw that chip away. They are not any goof for anything else.I hope this helps someone out there.Ken

    If you understand the schematic, it is easier. There are actually 5 different "clocks" . There are 2 that operate the DATA chip. These are labeled 7Mbar (pin 9) and 7M (pin 10). There is also a "chroma" clock that tells the system how to "sync" the colors. Then, from the DATA chip there is a "G" clock (pin 16). That goes into a flip flop circuit. This circuit produces 2 opposite pulses. When one is at 5 volts, the other is at Zero volts. Then the next time the "G" clock sends out a pulse, these switch. The 1st is then Zero and he other, 5V. These are "tuned" to turn synchronize all of the computers workings. If the timing is off, then these clocks may operate at different times, causing things to not work right.This could cause excessive heating in the chips also. That is why it seems like the DATA chip is bad when it really is not. The only way to check a DATA chip is to swap it with a chip in a working unit. If it then works...KEEP IT. you can either use it for a spare or try swapping the other custom chips 1 at a time, If one make the good unit stop working... TURN IT OFF IMMEDIATELY. Throw that chip away. They are not any goof for anything else.I hope this helps someone out there.Ken

This week, for the next episode of the Astrocast podcast, Paul and I will be discussing several letters that were sent to the Arcadian.  One letter, sent August 20, 1979, is from Jeff Frederiksen, the chief engineer behind the design of the Bally Professional Arcade hardware. It seems that this letter was accompanied by some hardware.  The letter simply states:

"The enclosed assemblies replace the 75361 clock driver, located in the oscillator shield. The failure of the 75361 is that the 6V high time after warm-up drops below 55ns causing the data chip to appear defective. If you do not have this sinking clock syndrome,  replacement is not necessary. I hope you find the enclosed hardware description useful."

You can view the original letter here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#JeffFrederiksenLetterAugust201979

If you understand the schematic, it is easier. There are actually 5 different "clocks" . There are 2 that operate the DATA chip. These are labeled 7Mbar (pin 9) and 7M (pin 10). There is also a "chroma" clock  that tells the system how to "sync" the colors. Then, from the DATA chip there is a "G" clock (pin 16). That goes into a flip flop circuit. This circuit produces 2 opposite pulses. When one is at 5 volts, the other is at Zero volts. Then the next time the  "G" clock sends out a pulse, these switch. The 1st is then Zero and he other, 5V. These are "tuned" to turn synchronize all of the computers workings. If the timing is off, then these clocks may operate at different times, causing things to not work right.

This could cause excessive heating in the chips also. That is why it seems like the DATA chip is bad when it really is not. The only way to check a DATA chip is to swap it with a chip in a working unit.  If it then works...KEEP IT. you can either use it for a spare or try swapping the other custom chips 1 at a time, If one make the good unit stop working... TURN IT OFF IMMEDIATELY. Throw that chip away. They are not any goof for anything else.

I hope this helps someone out there.

Ken

It is located between the DATA chip and the Cartridge slot plastic, inside the rectangular can. You would probably need to unsolder the top and to pry it off, you will need to bend up the tab that is under the cartridge plastic. It will then be staring you in the face. IF you were to under solder the 8 pins, it could then be pried off to expose the crystal, it's transistor and the 74s74 dual flip flop that drive the kludge PCB.Ken

If you understand the schematic, it is easier. There are actually 5 different "clocks" . There are 2 that operate the DATA chip. These are labeled 7Mbar (pin 9) and 7M (pin 10). There is also a "chroma" clock that tells the system how to "sync" the colors. Then, from the DATA chip there is a "G" clock (pin 16). That goes into a flip flop circuit. This circuit produces 2 opposite pulses. When one is at 5 volts, the other is at Zero volts. Then the next time the "G" clock sends out a pulse, these switch. The 1st is then Zero and he other, 5V. These are "tuned" to turn synchronize all of the computers workings. If the timing is off, then these clocks may operate at different times, causing things to not work right.

This could cause excessive heating in the chips also. That is why it seems like the DATA chip is bad when it really is not. The only way to check a DATA chip is to swap it with a chip in a working unit. If it then works...KEEP IT. you can either use it for a spare or try swapping the other custom chips 1 at a time, If one make the good unit stop working... TURN IT OFF IMMEDIATELY. Throw that chip away. They are not any goof for anything else.

I hope this helps someone out there.

Ken

The final round of the Astrocade High Score Club, Season 1, ended yesterday (February 6, 2017).  Thanks to everyone who participated!  I came in first place, but that's only because I played in every round and tried every bonus game.  Trust me, all those points aren't because I'm a good videogame player.


Congratulations to ranger_lennier (Paul Thacker), who came in second place and played nearly every game as well!  It has been a pleasure challenging (and being challenged by) all of you fine folks!

Here are the final results:

Astrocade High Score Club, Season 1 - Final Table

1  - BallyAlley     - 132 +  0 = 132
2  - ranger_lennier - 117 +  0 = 117
3  - nd2003grad     -  67 + 38 = 105 !
4  - Chris++        -  67 +  0 =  67
5  - roadrunner     -  41 + 19 =  60 !
6  - darthkur       -  31 +  0 =  31

7  - Brian Ciesicki -  15 +  0 =  15

7  - Lance Squire   -  15 +  0 =  15
8  - Benjamin Bauer -  10 +  0 =  10
9  - glazball       -  12 +  0 =  12
10 - billnewsome    -   9 +  0 =   9
11 - bwbauer        -   7 +  0 =   7
12 - Orion Miller   -   6 +  0 =   6
13 - jblenkle       -   3 +  0 =   3
13 - tripletopper   -   3 +  0 =   3

! - Received bonus points from round 14 (the "catch-up" round).


I think that a few of these names in this final high score table may be duplicates.  For instance, I'm pretty sure that "bwbauer" and Benjamin Bauer are the same person, which means that these two scores need to be combined.  Please alert me (in the thread below) if you have two scores included in the above list.

You can read my complete comments and posting about the final scores here:


http://atariage.com/forums/topic/261928-hsc01-final-standings/


Season 2 of the HSC will be starting soon-- so get your Astrocade (or emulation) set up and your Bally hand controllers ready for battle!

Adam

15052:
Solar Conqueror is the main game for Round 1 of the second season of the Astrocade High Score Club. This game, which takes place in space with you controlling a ship that must shoot baddies, reminds me of Blast Droids, the last game that we played in season 1 of the HSC. However, the similarities are slight. Whereas Blast Droids was a chore to play, Solar Conqueror is fun!

The BASIC bonus game, Space Gauntlet, is an another game that takes place in in the depths of the dark forbidden universe that teams with, you got it!, more baddies. This game, while released on tape for both Bally BASIC and "AstroBASIC," the program has only been archived in 300-baud Bally BASIC format. This means that you'll need the Bally Tape interface to load it.

Season 3, Round 1 will last about three weeks. The round ends on Sunday, February 26'th at 8pm MST.


For complete details of this round, visit the thread in the AtariAge forums, here:


http://atariage.com/forums/topic/261983-hsc02-round-1-solar-conqueror-space-gauntlet/


Solar Conqueror is one of the best games in the Astrocade library, so come join the fun and play a few rounds of this game over the next few weeks.


Adam

Over the past three days, I have added 23 different WaveMakers Bally BASIC 300-baud programs to BallyAlley.com.  Most of these programs have been previously available in non-digitally archived format.

On October 17, 2016, Paul Thacker finished converting all of these programs to a digitally archived format; this has two benefits.  One: it makes the programs load more reliably via the 300-baud tape interface.  Two: it makes the compressed programs take up far less storage space.  For instance, these programs previously took up about 140MB (Yes, megabytes!).  Now they all take up less than 1MB (about 890K to be more precise).

The newly added programs are:

1) Backgammon (300-Baud)
2) Brick 'N the Wall (300-Baud)
3) Clue (300-Baud)
4) Guitar Course (300-Baud)
5) Horse Race (300-Baud)
6) Invasion Force (300-Baud)
7) Lookout for the Bull! (300-Baud)
8) Max (Robot from Space) (300-Baud)
9) Maze Race and Obstacle Course (300-Baud)
10) Mazemaker I and II (300-Baud)
11) Memory Doodle (300-Baud)
12) Mouse in the Hat (300-Baud)
13) Music Composer (300-Baud)
14) Obstacle Course Tournament (300-Baud)
15) Pack-Rat I and Pack-Rat II (300-Baud)
16) Perversion (300-Baud)
17) Sideswipe (300-Baud)
18) Slot Machine (300-Baud)
19) Space Chase (300-Baud)
20) Speed Math / Note Match (300-Baud)
21) WaveMakers' Fortune Teller (300-Baud)
22) Wavemakers Tapes Are (300-Baud) - New to BallyAlley.com
23) Yahtzee (300-Baud)

The WaveMakers 300-baud download area is here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/WaveMakers/WaveMakers.html

There is only one 300-baud program that has not yet been digitally archived: Whiz Quiz.  Paul and I have both put this program aside because it will take a very long time to digitally process and check it.  I guess we'll get to it eventually, but nether of us really wants to make sure that all 250 questions load and process correctly.

If you'd like more information about the archiving process of any of these programs, then read Paul's notes from his original email about finishing a large part of the WaveMakers Bally BASIC archiving project (see below).

Thanks for archiving all of these programs, Paul.

Have fun, everybody!

Adam

From: ballyalley@yahoogroups.com <ballyalley@yahoogroups.com> on behalf of lennier_of_the_minbari@yahoo.com [ballyalley] <ballyalley@yahoogroups.com>

Subject: [ballyalley] WaveMakers 300 baud programs--now improved with digital processing!

I've used the 300 baud processing tools to digitally process a number of WaveMakers programs. These were previously only available as raw recordings. These are smaller and should load more reliably. Most programs now on-line come from the Mike Peace's master  tapes. I've also sorted through whatever I could find from my backlog of recordings from these alternate sources--Brett Bilbrey's tape collection, Bob Fabris's tape collection, Jack Flynn's tape collection, and Ken Lill's tape collection. These did reveal  alternate versions, including a version of Fortune Teller that doesn't crash like the version on the master tapes does.

We still need to test Whiz Quiz--that has a huge number of loads. I also have some tapes from Mike White I've never looked at, so there could be alternates on those. But these have been in progress too long already, so I'll go ahead and send Adam what I've  got.

Here are my complete notes on the programs.

Backgammon (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Backgammon (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. The code differs in several places, but it's not immediately obvious that it plays differently.

Backgammon (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a2] - Found on commercial tape in Jack Flynn's tape collection. The main program is identical to the version from the master tapes, but the introduction program is slightly different.

Brick 'N The Wall (1982)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD) - found on hand-labeled tape in Bob Fabris's collection.

Clue (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Clue (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - archived from commercial tape in Jack Flynn's collection. Slightly different than version from master tapes.

Guitar Course Introduction (1980)(WaveMakers)(PD)[spoken] - This is a spoken introduction from Mike Peace found in Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. It's addressed to George, perhaps George Moses.

Guitar Tuning & Guitar Course (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[Guitar Course tape side 1][From Master Tapes]

Guitar Tuning & Guitar Course (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[Guitar Course tape side 1][a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. It's formatted differently and there are a few code differences, but it's not immediately obvious that it plays differently.

Horse Race (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Invasion Force (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[freebee on Lookout For The Bull! II tape][From Master Tapes], Invasion Force (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[freebee on Pack-Rat II tape][From Master Tapes] - The code in the two versions is slightly different.

Lookout For The Bull! (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Lookout For The Bull! II (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Max (Robot From Space) (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Mazemaker (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[freebee on Flying Ace tape][From Master Tapes] - This is slightly different than the versions previously digitally archived.

Mazemaker (with introduction) (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. It seems closest to "Mazemaker (with introduction) (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)", but has some formatting and code differences.

Mazemaker II (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[freebee on Perversion tape][From Master Tapes]

Mazemaker II (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - found on tape in Bob Fabris's collection hand-labeled "WaveMakers Extras - Natasia The Fortune Teller, Mazemaker II, Memory Doodle". The code is slightly different than the version from the master tapes.

Maze Race, Obstacle Course (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Memory Doodle (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD) - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. The comments describe it as a "no-charge extra". I didn't find a 300 baud version of this program on the master tapes. I also found a version of this on a tape in  Bob Fabris's collection hand-labeled "WaveMakers Extras - Natasia The Fortune Teller, Mazemaker II, Memory Doodle" which appears to be identical aside from archiving errors.

Mouse In The Hat (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Mouse In The Hat (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection.  It's a little different than the version from the master tapes, but it's mostly just formatting. However, it doesn't work correctly. You can never kill the  mice. It's missing a direct setting of the variable P, so it may have been improperly copied.

Music Composer (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[with Oh Susanna][From Master Tapes] - To compose music, turn the knob to choose duration and push joystick up or down to move notes on scale. Push joystick right to place note, or pull trigger to place a rest.  To go back to main menu, push joystick down until you're off the scale, then pull trigger.

Music Composer (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[with Oh Susanna][a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. There are both code and formatting differences from the version on the master tapes.

Music Composer (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[with The Man On The Flying Trapeze] - I created this file by combining two recordings from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection--"Music Composer (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[with Oh Susanna][a]" (with the music  data removed) and "The Man On The Flying Trapeze (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[for Music Composer]". On the WaveMakers master tapes, I found a 2000 baud version of The Man On The Flying Trapeze, but no 300 baud version.

Note Match & Chord Progressions (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[Guitar Course tape side 2][From Master Tapes] - crashes with certain combinations. I checked another copy from Brett Bilbrey's collection, and the code is identical.

Obstacle Course Tournament (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Obstacle Course Tournament (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This is from Brett Bilbrey's tape collection. It's a little different than the version from the master tapes, but it's mostly just formatting.

Obstacle Course Tournament (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a2] - This is from a commercial tape in Jack Flynn's collection. It's slightly different than the other versions.

Pack-Rat (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Pack-Rat (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This version was found in Ken Lill's tape collection, and is slightly different than the version from the WaveMakers master tapes.

Pack-Rat II (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Perversion (1980)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[From Master Tapes]

Pack-Rat II (1981)(WaveMakers)(300 baud)(PD)[a] - This version was found in both Brett Bilbrey's and Ken Lill's tape collections, and is slightly different than the version from the WaveMakers master tapes.

I have added the BASIC listing of John Collin's 1980 Bally BASIC adventure game, Bally's Alley.  Yes, the game is called Bally's Alley and it has been added to BallyAlley.com.  That's sort of weird, I know.


Let me share a short story about how this program ended up on the website.  Last night Paul, Michael and I recorded the Bally Alley Astrocast #8.  We reviewed the cartridge Blast Droids and a BASIC game called Haunted House.  We were talking about adventure games written in BASIC.  One that came up is called Treasures of Cathy by John Collins.  I mentioned that I thought this was part of a trilogy, but this didn't ring a bell with Paul.  However, Paul being the investigative fellow that he is looked into this off-the-cuff remark I made.  He came up with the title Bally's Alley, which he noticed was available as a type-in listing in the Bob Fabris Collection.


As far as I can tell, we don't have this program on tape at all (in either RAW or archived format).  I've glanced through the BASIC listing; this game will be tough to type in.  First, the program will have to be typed in from the typed BASIC listing (it's not a hand-written listing, thankfully).  After the program is entered, variables A-Z and the @ array (elements 0-99) must be loaded by hand from a hard-to-read handwritten sheet of paper (hopefully, all these numbers were written down correctly).  I don't plan to type this one in, but there's no reason the listing shouldn't be online; maybe somehow will try typing this one in someday.

You can download the type-in listing here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#BallysAlleyJohnCollinsBBTypeIn


Here are the instructions that I've OCRed and compiled for the game, Bally's Alley:

Bally's Alley (An Adventure Game)
By John Collins
1980

Availability

Bally's Alley was offered for sale on tape in the classified ads section of the
Arcadian 2, no. 7 (May 19, 1980): 66.

Game Description

This game description is from an advertisement in the Summer 1982 issue of the
Bally / Astro Professional Arcade Software and Hardware Sourcebook:

Bally's Alley - An adventure game; one player.  Game can last for days or weeks; can save at any point for restart; can go in nine directions; find the ten treasures and return to house; can only carry four treasures at one time. Each move subtracts a point.  A magic word-sound-color will be helpful.

Program Documentation by John Collins


This is the first in a series of adventure programs I hope to write.  This program is a very complicated game.  It may take days or even weeks to complete.  However, it is designed to let you stop at any point in game- break the program- insert a new tape (be sure that it's a new tape so not to destroy the original tape)- type in GOTO 9000 -turn the recorder on to record and press GO.  This will make a new tape-relisting of program and present values of the variables.  To restart the game, just use the new tape.

When the game starts, you will see a menu.  Enter one of the numbers 1, 2, 3, or 4 and press GO.  If you enter 1, you will see a new menu for which directions you can go.  If you had entered 2, you would be able to type in words which may have special meaning like- TAKE KEYS.  If you had entered 3, it will identify which treasures you are carrying.  You can carry a maximum of four treasures at one time.  You get some points for picking up the treasure, but they will be subtracted if you do not drop the treasures in the right room.  The fourth thing on the menu is the score.  Each room you go into, each time, will cost you a point.  However, the treasures are worth many points so do not be discouraged.  When you see the menu for directions; you can go in one of nine directions (no southeast).  Many times when you enter a location you cannot return in the opposite direction.  Normally there are two directions forward and two directions backwards from a location.  Some of the locations have the same name.  A magic word - sound - color will be helpful.



This sounds like a neat program, doesn't it?  Thanks for pointing it out, Paul!


Enjoy!

Adam

I'd like to use Ballybin to create plain binary files for a BASICart.  Ken explained to me on the phone the BASIC procedure of how to make a BASICart, which are:


1) Open a previously made BASICart in a hex editor.  I'm using the BASICart called "Sloshed! (1986)(New Image and Mike White)(PD).bin as my test program.


2) Erase the top half of the 8K ROM ($1000-$1FFF)


3) Convert a BASIC WAV file into a binary file.


4) Place the converted binary file at $1000 in the BASICart and you're done.


The problem is that I don't know how to use Ballybin to convert the WAV file into the proper binary format.  The binary format that Ballybin uses is sort of a mix between XML and a binary file, which won't work with a BASICart.


Any help that anyone can offer would be useful to me.

There are 508 300-baud Bally BASIC programs on BallyAlley.com.  Not all of these are actually BASIC programs.  Some of the software are machine language programs that load though Bally BASIC, while others are archives of several programs put together on one tape (for instance, Mike White's 300-Baud Demo Tape).

I checked how many of these 300-baud programs have NOT been digitally archived, and there are only 24 of the 508 programs left.  That means that 95.3% of the 508 programs available in 300-baud format on BallyAlley.com has been archived!  Paul Thacker did nearly all of the digital archiving; thanks, Paul!

This isn't to say that all Bally BASIC programs are nearly archived-- that's not so at all, but of the ones that HAVE been archived (recorded from tape, or typed into BASIC), there are only about 5% left to clean up digitally to make perfect copies.

Here is the list of the 24 programs on BallyAlley.com that have not yet been digitally archived:

Programs from the Arcadian:

1)  4d2_(300-baud)_[rusty_blommaert,_et_al].zip
2)  Frog (1982)(Bob Wiseman)(BB).zip
3)  Fudd (1982)(Bob Wiseman)(BB).zip
4)  Stranded On Rigel 5 (Sean Walsh).zip
5)  telling_time_(300-baud)_[bob_hensel].zip

Programs from Cursor/BASIC Express:

6)  Line Resequencer (Mike Peace)(BB).zip

Programs by  Esoterica:

7)  big_city_slick_(300)_[esoterica_ltd].zip
8)  bomb_squad_(300)_[esoterica_ltd].zip
9)  garbersville_(300)_[esoterica_ltd].zip
10) great_american_jigsaw,_the_(300)_[esoterica_ltd].zip
11) mini_golf_(300)_[esoterica_ltd].zip
12) star_trek_(300)_[esoterica_ltd].zip
13) ten_pins_(300)_[esoterica_ltd].zip
14) treasure_island_(300)_[esoterica_ltd].zip
15) wildcatter_(300)_[esoterica_ltd].zip

Miscellaneous Programs

16) 3 Tone Music (with Star Wars music) (198x)(Brett Bilbrey)(300 baud)(PD).zip
17) Goldfish Demo (The Bit Fiddlers)(300 Baud).zip
18) Mike's 300-Baud Demo Tape (Michael White).zip
19) quadra_(300-baud)_[mike_white].zip
20) Sonic Satellite (1979)(George Hale)(300 baud).zip
21) video_wallpaper_(300-baud)_[jay_fenton].zip
22) z-80_mini-course_(300-baud)_[barry_ellerson].zip
23) ZZZ-UNK (enter numbers) (19xx)(300 baud).zip
           
Programs by WaveMakers

24) Whiz Quiz- Common Knowledge (WaveMakers)[300 baud].zip

I've slowly added Paul's digitally archived programs over the years to replace the non-digitally archived programs, but I had no idea that he'd done nearly finished archiving it all!

Adam

15078:
When Paul, Michael and I were recording a segment of the Astrocast podcast this past Sunday night, I mentioned that I thought that the program The Treasures of Cathy by John Collins was part of a trilogy.  Paul emailed me the next day and said that he thought I might be talking about the unarchived game (with an available BASIC listing) called Bally's Alley.  That title sounded about right, but I wasn't so sure it was correct.  However, Paul's suggest did give me a reason to upload the BASIC listing for the game, which is why I added Bally's Alley yesterday to the website.


Today, quite by accident, I came up with the actual title I was thinking about on Sunday.  While going through BASIC listings from the Fabris Collection, I ran across the original program submission letter for The Crown of Zeus by Todd Johnson.  This program was originally published in the November 1982 issue of the Arcadian.  It seemed to be quite popular with readers.


According to ads in Arcadian 5, no. 1 (Nov. 5, 1982): 9. and Arcadian 4, no. 10 (Aug. 06, 1982): 103., The Crown of Zeus is the first in a series of four programs that take place on the planet Gibeleous. The other three games in the series are available only on tape and are called:

1) The Rescue of Catherine
2) Escape from Rantanam IV
3) The Tower of Machor


So, I was wrong: the series of programs make up not a trilogy, but a tetralogy.  It was the similar titles of Treasures of Cathy and The Rescue of Catherine that made me confuse the two programs.  I'm surprised that I remembered this tid-bit of information at all.  As far as I'm aware, there are no versions of the sequels to The Crown of Zeus available in any format (tape or BASIC listing).


That Bally's software library is vast and full of programs that barely were distributed at all.  It seems that many of these lesser-known programs, many of which were the work of quite talented amateur programmers, have fallen through the archiving cracks and are not available anywhere, that is... unless you happen to have some of them!

15082:
I have added two different sets of maps for Todd Johnson's game, The Crown of Zeus-- which was published in Arcadian 5, no. 1 (Nov. 5, 1982): 7-10.


1) I added The Crown of Zeus castle map by Edward Mahoney.  This was sent to Bob Fabris on April 20 1983.  An excerpt from Edward's letter says:

"The reason I'm writing is to share with you the attached drawings of what I think the castle in The Crown of Zeus (volume 5:1:7) by Todd Johnson looks like.  I would like to know if anyone has written this program to produce graphics on the screen of the movement from room-to-room.  I think this would be a great program to see with graphic displays.  Perhaps, some of those great programmers that write in the Arcadian can publish game graphics for this program."


http://www.ballyalley.com/tape_manuals/misc/misc.html#CrownofZeusMapEdwardMahoney

II) I added floor plans for Todd Johnson's The Crown of Zeus.  These floor plans were created by Kent Brenden and sent to the Arcadian on July 9, 1983.  Here is an excerpt from Kent's letter:

"The graph paper enclosed contains the floor plans [for The Crown of Zeus]. Each level is labeled, each room is numbered with its exits shown.  The set of lines that extends from one room to another indicate a passageway from one room to another.  If the set of lines don't go into another room (as with room 13, level 3), this indicates that you can leave the room but once out of that room you can't reenter that room."

Kent made some changes to the program (which are included in his letter).  These changes make the game a little easier to play (without the need to reload the game).  Included in the letter is a hint for Artillery Duel (probably the BASIC version of the game), which makes it nearly impossible for the other player to hit you.  Ken also talks about File Searcher, scrolling, Magic RAM, and the CHRDIS (Character Display) on-board subroutine.


http://www.ballyalley.com/tape_manuals/misc/misc.html#CrownofZeusMapKentBrenden


These maps by these two different people are pretty cool.  They remind me of the maps that I created for myself when I first played The Legend of Zelda on the NES back in the 80s.

The CoCo video mode is "SG12". This mode is created through the
combination of the 6847 VDG and the 6883 SAM chips. The MP1000 doesn't
have the 6883 so it won't have this particular mode. It does do some
funny wiring with the 6847, so there might be other interesting things
to do there...

> John, how long did it take you to program Fahrhall?  For some reason, Fahrhall rings a bell with me.  I think that maybe Randy might have mentioned it on his Floppy Days podcast.  Is the source code for your game available?  Is this the first game that you made?

Fahrfall was originally a 1-month RetroChallenge project, back in
January of 2012. But even after being a winner in that event, Fahrfall
still wasn't quite "done". I worked on it on and off (more off than
on, really) for as much as two years afterwards, during which time
I also took it to several vintage computing and "maker" events for
play testing by real people. It's funny, some people like the game
and some don't. But there are a few people that absolutely love it. :-)

Anyway, yes, Randy interviewed me on Floppy Days a couple of years
ago. It probably is the first game I made, certainly the first one as a
"retro programmer". The source code is not available, primarily because
I wanted to preserve the "Fahrve" character for future games. I have
always said that if you _really_ want the source, then come and talk
to me -- so far, no one has bothered with that part.

At this point, I sometimes feel tired of Fahrfall. There was a port of
Fahrfall to the Apple 2, and there have been several add-on projects
(including making cartridge cases, labels, boxes, etc) to the point
of making me wonder if I know how to do anything else! Still, it
seems there is always something in Fahrfall calling me back...

it shows-up on the Astrocade!

Let me share a short story about how this program ended up on the website.  Last night Paul, Michael and I recorded the Bally Alley Astrocast #8.  We reviewed the cartridgeBlast Droids and a BASIC game called Haunted House.  We were talking about adventure games written in BASIC.  One that came up is calledTreasures of Cathy by John Collins.  I mentioned that I thought this was part of a trilogy, but this didn't ring a bell with Paul.  However, Paul being the investigative fellow that he is looked into this off-the-cuff remark I made.  He came up with the title Bally's Alley, which he noticed was available as a type-in listing in the Bob Fabris Collection.



As far as I can tell, we don't have this program on tape at all (in either RAW or archived format).  I've glanced through the BASIC listing; this game will be tough to type in.  First, the program will have to be typed in from the typed BASIC listing (it's not a hand-written listing, thankfully).  After the program is entered, variables A-Z and the @ array (elements 0-99) must be loaded by hand from a hard-to-read handwritten sheet of paper (hopefully, all these numbers were written downcorrectly).  I don't plan to type this one in, but there's no reason the listing shouldn't be online; maybe somehow will try typing this one in someday.


You can download the type-in listing here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#BallysAlleyJohnCollinsBBTypeIn


Here are the instructions that I've OCRed and compiled for the game, Bally's Alley:


Bally's Alley (An Adventure Game)
By John Collins
1980

Availability

Bally's Alley was offered for sale on tape in the classified ads section of the
Arcadian 2, no. 7 (May 19, 1980): 66.

Game Description

This game description is from an advertisement in the Summer 1982 issue of the
Bally / Astro Professional Arcade Software and Hardware Sourcebook:

Bally's Alley - An adventure game; one player.  Game can last for days or weeks; can save at any point for restart; can go in nine directions; find the ten treasures and return to house; can only carry four treasures at one time. Each move subtracts a point.  A magic word-sound-color will be helpful.

Program Documentation by John Collins


This is the first in a series of adventure programs I hope to write.  This program is a very complicated game.  It may take days or even weeks to complete.  However, it is designed to let you stop at any point in game- break the program- insert a new tape (be sure that it's a new tape so not to destroy the original tape)- type in GOTO 9000 -turn the recorder on to record and press GO.  This will make a new tape-relisting of program and present values of the variables.  To restart the game, just use the new tape.


When the game starts, you will see a menu.  Enter one of the numbers 1, 2, 3, or 4 and press GO.  If you enter 1, you will see a new menu for which directions you can go.  If you had entered 2, you would be able to type in words which may have special meaning like- TAKE KEYS.  If you had entered 3, it will identify which treasures you are carrying.  You can carry a maximum of four treasures at one time.  You get some points for picking up the treasure, but they will be subtracted if you do not drop the treasures in the right room.  The fourth thing on the menu is the score.  Each room you go into, each time, will cost you a point.  However, the treasures are worth many points so do not be discouraged.  When you see the menu for directions; you can go in one of nine directions (no southeast).  Many times when you enter a location you cannot return in the opposite direction.  Normally there are two directions forward and two directions backwards from a location.  Some of the locations have the same name.  A magic word - sound - color will be helpful.



This sounds like a neat program, doesn't it?  Thanks for pointing it out, Paul!





Enjoy!


Adam

Star Battle is the main game for round 2 of the second season of the Astrocade High Score Club.


Star Battle is a 2K cartridge released by Bally Mfg. Corp. in 1979. It is part of the Action/Skills Series. It was re-released in 1981 by Astrovision, Inc. Unlike last round's game, Solar Conqueror, which was among the last games released for the Astrocade, Star Battle was among the first of them.


In the Bally/Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ, Michael White states that Star Battle is a port of the Bally/Midway 1980 coin-op arcade game Space Encounters. Space Encounters was a B&W game that used a color overlay; the games do indeed look very similar.  Here is the Star Battle's description from the front of the manual:

"An exciting race through space in a running battle with enemy star ships. Three dimensional screen action looks like you're plunging through a time warp on your way to hyperspace! Fire your missiles and take evasive action to avoid enemy lasers! You have full control over your spacecraft's speed and direction-- and you can play to any score for long or short games!"


The BASIC bonus game is Down the Trench, released in 1979 by Sebree's Computing (programmed by Timothy Hays).  It is a perfect pairing for Star Battle; I just couldn't pass it up for this round. Down the Trench, like Star Battle, is another game that takes place in the depths of the Star Wars movie universe.


As far as I'm aware, Down the Trench was only released on tape for Bally BASIC in 300-baud format. This means that you'll need the Bally Tape interface to load it; it won't load into "AstroBASIC."

Down the Trench is featured in an ad that says:


"Down the Trench - 1 player. Six levels of difficulty. This program has [many] branches so that many things can happen. It may take you an hour to finally succeed in destroying the Death Star and move to a higher level of difficulty. After you evade the enemies laser shots, you engage your flight computer and wait to fire as a 3-dimensional representation of your target moves up on you. But that isn't all! Spectacular explosions and graphic movement with its unbeatable documentation make this a unique simulation/game."

You don't need a working Astrocade console, as you can play Star Battle easily in the Astrocade emulator included in MAME.     When Paul, Michael and I were recording a segment of the Astrocast podcast this past Sunday night, I mentioned that I thought that the programThe Treasures of Cathy by John Collins was part of a trilogy.  Paul emailed me the next day and said that he thought I might be talking about the unarchived game (with an available BASIC listing) calledBally's Alley.  That title sounded about right, but I wasn't so sure it was correct.  However, Paul's suggest did give me a reason to upload the BASIC listing for the game, which is why I addedBally's Alley yesterday to the website.
Today, quite by accident, I came up with the actual title I was thinking about on Sunday.  While going through BASIC listings from the Fabris Collection, I ran across the original program submission letter forThe Crown of Zeus by Todd Johnson.  This program was originally published in the November 1982 issue of theArcadian.  It seemed to be quite popular with readers.
According to ads in Arcadian 5, no. 1 (Nov. 5, 1982): 9. and Arcadian 4, no. 10 (Aug. 06, 1982): 103.,The Crown of Zeus is the first in a series of four programs that take place on the planet Gibeleous. The other three games in the series are available only on tape and are called:

1) The Rescue of Catherine
2) Escape from Rantanam IV
3) The Tower of Machor

So, I was wrong: the series of programs make up not a trilogy, but a tetralogy.  It was the similar titles ofTreasures of Cathy and The Rescue of Catherine that made me confuse the two programs.  I'm surprised that I remembered this tid-bit of information at all.  As far as I'm aware, there are no versions of the sequels toThe Crown of Zeus available in any format (tape or BASIC listing).
That Bally's software library is vast and full of programs that barely were distributed at all.  It seems that many of these lesser-known programs, many of which were the work of quite talented amateur programmers, have fallen through the archiving cracks and are not available anywhere, that is... unless you happen to have some of them!

Adam

I played a four-player game of War at the Louisville Arcade Expo this weekend.  We played eight rounds total, and it was a really close match.  Out of the maximum number of 29 games in an 8 round match (if the players score 7,7,7,8), we played 26 total rounds:

Attached is a picture of our final number of rounds won in the complete game.  The players were (from left to right):

15097:
I have added Michael Matte's hand-written Z80 source code and instructions for "High-Res 'Test Rotate' Routine" to BallyAlley.com.  He sent this to me in the mail yesterday.  Michael just wrote this routine this year.

The "Rotate" routine rotates a 4x4 pixel pattern that resides in the Astrocade's user RAM. This routine was written for use on a modified high resolution Astrocade, but (this is the cool part), this routine can be modified for use on a normal Astrocade.

For those unaware how cool this is, the "Nutting Manual" (sort of the Astrocade's programming Bible) says that the rotate function of the Magic System does not function on a low-res Astrocade console. Specifically, page 98 of the manual says, "the rotator can only be used in commercial [hi-res] mode." However, Michael discovered that it is just a case that the on-board graphic subroutines in the Astrocade's ROM do not support the Rotate function. The Astrocade's hardware does support the rotate function, but the user has to write the routine to tell the hardware to rotate the pattern. The documentation included with this hand-written Z80 source code provides the needed changes to use the rotate function on a low-res Astrocade unit.


The routine, as written, does the following:

1) Sets a high-res Astrocade screen map to "High-Res" mode.
2) Clears the top 10 lines on screen.
3) Outputs "Rotate" bit to Magic Register.
4) Sets Magic address to display rotated pattern midway at top of screen.
5) Writes the initial pattern a second time at the same exact Magic address.
6) The Astrocade hardware then rotates the initial pattern 90 degrees.
7) The Z80 halts and continues executing NOP's until the Astrocade Reset button is pressed.


I haven't tested this code, but Michael used it in both hi-res and low-res modes of his modified Astroacade.

You can download the hand-written source code here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_homebrew/ml_homebrew.html#MLHomebrewHighResTestRotateRoutine


I've already re-typed this entire rotate document and source code (including all the documentation and comments) and assembled it using Zmac with no errors.  However, I have not yet compared the output code against the hand-written listing.  I'll do this over the next few days.  After that, I'll modify the source code to try the routine on a low-res system, then it's off to test the routine under the Astrocade emulator, and (eventually) under the Machine Language Manager cartridge.  Maybe by the weekend, or possibly next week, I'll have this done.


For all those Z80 programmers out there, I'd say this is pretty awesome!

Adam
15098:
I have added Palo Alto Tiny BASIC, Version 3 by Li-Chen Wang. This article (which includes the source code and assembly listing) is excerpted from pages 58-88 of the 1977 book PCC's Reference Book of Personal And Home Computing, Edited by Dwight McCabe.  Paul gave me this book this past weekend-- so... thanks, Paul!


For those not already aware, Bally BASIC and "AstroBASIC" are a superset of the original Palo Alto Tiny BASIC.

This version of Li-Chen Wang's Palo Alto Tiny BASIC will run on either the 8080 or Z-80, and only uses 2K of core memory. It contains a number of nice features including command abbreviations and error messages. At the end of the listing is a cross reference table for symbols used in the program and also the object code for the program. For further information on Tiny BASIC languages, see Dr. Dobb's Journal, Volume 1.


http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/ml_source.html#PaloAltoTinyBASIC3SourceCodepdf


I've seen various versions of the source code for Tiny BASIC, but I've never come across version 3.0 before I saw the listing in this book.  At about 2K in size, this version of Tiny BASIC is very small (well, duh!).  It's not wonder that Jay Fenton was able to expand upon this version of Tiny BASIC when he ported it to the Astrocade as a 4K cartridge.  Bally BASIC includes numerous editions to the language, including the ability to work with graphics.


I looked around for the the 8080 source code in an assembler-ready format for this version of Tiny BASIC, but I couldn't find it.


Has anyone ever compared all of the differences (and similarities) between Tiny BASIC, Bally BASIC and "AstroBASIC?"


Adam

15102:
Michael Di Salvo wrote:
>>
with RAM being RAM, if you plugged in a 64k expanded RAM board into the console, couldn't the system use that to run in high resolution mode?
>>


I'm aware that both Ken and Lance already just answered Michael's hi-res question with (basically) "Nope, sorry; there can be no use of the hi-res mode without internal modification to the Astrocade".  This question will likely always creek up from time to time because its such an intriguing possibility.  In fact, the "Hi-Res Astrocade" used to possibly be the most commonly asked question on the Yahoo group.  There was a time when the answer was a murky; when people weren't 100% sure if it could be done or not.


Back in 2001, Tony Miller, one of the designers of the Astrocade, answered this question (with what would probably be now be referred to as a) white paper on the Astrocade console and it's arcade cousins.  He called his paper, simply, the Bally Professional Arcade Video Hardware.

It is a description of the Bally Professional Arcade video hardware and its associated coin-operated hardware.  The detailed, 25-page document, describes how the Bally Arcade/Astrocade video hardware works.  This was created to dispel the rumor that an unmodified, low-res (160x102 pixel-resolution) Bally Arcade unit can display commercial resolution ("hi-res," 320x204 pixel-resolution) video.

The primary sources of information used to write this paper include the "Nutting Manual," U.S. Patents 4,301,503 and 4,475172, the Sea Wolf II arcade game schematics and the Bally Service Manual.

If you're interested in the details, you can read them in the pdf, here:


http://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/BPA%20Video%20Hardware%20FAQ/Bally_Professional_Arcade_Video_Hardware%20(2001)(Tony%20Miller).pdf


I've looked through this document before, but I can't honestly say that I understand most of it.  Still, it's worth bringing up because Tony did such a great service to the Astrocade community by writing this paper.

Adam

Today I released the newest episode of the Astrocade podcast: Bally Alley Astrocast: Episode 8 - Blast Droids and Haunted House.  You can download it here and read the extensive show notes, here:

http://ballyalleyastrocast.libsyn.com/bally-alley-astrocast-episode-8-blast-droids-and-haunted-house


In episode 8 of the Bally Alley Astrocast, Paul, Michael and I review the 4K Blast Droids cartridge that Esoterica released in 1983. This game was written by Dan Drescher, and J.P. Curran. We also review the BASIC game Haunted House released by New Image in 1981.

Paul and I discuss the contents and programs included in the August and September 1979 issues of the Arcadian newsletters. We also read feedback from Arcadian readers that sent letters and postcards to Bob Fabris concerning the July 1979 survey question that asked if users would purchase a third-party keyboard and RAM upgrade. Lastly, we cover about ten letters that cover general topics that were sent to the Arcadian from late July to September 1979.

This episode is about three hours and fifteen minutes long.

Enjoy listening to the podcast.  If you have any feedback, feel free to post it here or email me.

Adam

Star Battle is the main game for round 2 of the second season of the Astrocade High Score Club.


Star Battle is a 2K cartridge released by Bally Mfg. Corp. in 1979. It is part of the Action/Skills Series. It was re-released in 1981 by Astrovision, Inc. Unlike last round's game, Solar Conqueror, which was among the last games released for the Astrocade, Star Battle was among the first of them.


In the Bally/Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ, Michael White states that Star Battle is a port of the Bally/Midway 1980 coin-op arcade game Space Encounters. Space Encounters was a B&W game that used a color overlay; the games do indeed look very similar.  Here is the Star Battle's description from the front of the manual:

"An exciting race through space in a running battle with enemy star ships. Three dimensional screen action looks like you're plunging through a time warp on your way to hyperspace! Fire your missiles and take evasive action to avoid enemy lasers! You have full control over your spacecraft's speed and direction-- and you can play to any score for long or short games!"


The BASIC bonus game is Down the Trench, released in 1979 by Sebree's Computing (programmed by Timothy Hays).  It is a perfect pairing for Star Battle; I just couldn't pass it up for this round. Down the Trench, like Star Battle, is another game that takes place in the depths of the Star Wars movie universe.


As far as I'm aware, Down the Trench was only released on tape for Bally BASIC in 300-baud format. This means that you'll need the Bally Tape interface to load it; it won't load into "AstroBASIC."

Down the Trench is featured in an ad that says:


"Down the Trench - 1 player. Six levels of difficulty. This program has [many] branches so that many things can happen. It may take you an hour to finally succeed in destroying the Death Star and move to a higher level of difficulty. After you evade the enemies laser shots, you engage your flight computer and wait to fire as a 3-dimensional representation of your target moves up on you. But that isn't all! Spectacular explosions and graphic movement with its unbeatable documentation make this a unique simulation/game."

This round ends Sunday, March 19'th at 8pm MST.  Post all scores in the AtariAge.com Astrocade High Score Club sub-forum.  Scores posted on the Bally Alley discussion group will not be accepted.


Come join the Astrocade fun in the high score club area on AtariAge.  The complete details for round two, including all the ways to score bonus points, pictures, photos and many links, are here:


http://atariage.com/forums/topic/262779-hsc02-round-2-star-battle-down-the-trench/


You don't need a working Astrocade console, as you can play Star Battle easily in the Astrocade emulator included in MAME.  There were four people who played in round 1 of this season's Astrocade High Score Club.  Let's see if we can get a few more people over there for round 2.  I'd love to see Lance Squire, Ken Lill, and Michael Di Salvo participate.  Heck, I'd love to see you all participate!

I added CHRDIS by Mike Skala. This tutorial series, and its accompanying programs, were published across three issues of the Arcadian: CHRDIS I. Arcadian 5, no. 1 (Nov. 5, 1982): 14-15., CHRDIS II. Arcadian 5, no. 2 (Dec. 3, 1982): 37., and CHRDIS III. Arcadian 5, no. 4 (Feb. 18, 1983): 72.

This three-part CHRDIS article describes how to use the Bally Arcade's built-in Character Display routine from within Bally BASIC. I think that the programs included in the article are "AstroBASIC"-only, but the general principles talked about in the article should apply to Bally BASIC too.

"I've seen quite a bit of software lately utilizing the Graphic Character Maker, a machine code routine that Arcadian has published in the past year. This allowed us to use a display routine from the on-board ROM and put complex graphics on the screen instantly, rather than a slow series of BOX and LINE commands. The major drawback here was when moving the graphics, erasing and redrawing: it left us with considerable flashing or blinking. If you have been with us for a while, you know that we are continually evolving and improving; the following tutorial is our new generation of screen animation for the Astrocade!"


You can read the article here:

Muncher (also sometimes called Munchie) is the main game for round 3 of the second season of the Astrocade High Score Club.  Muncher is an excellent Pac-Man clone.  This game is one of my favorite games for the Astrocade, and it's a shame that it wasn't released (probably) due to Atari's legal department making threats to sue companies that made copy-cat games.

The BASIC bonus game is New Image's game Nam-Cap, which was released on tape for $10.95 in December of 1982. "Nam-Cap" is the name "Pac-Man" spelled backwards. That's pretty-much how this game plays too: instead of eating dots, you "up-chuck" them onto the screen.

Come join the current round and play these two games on AtariAge.com:


http://atariage.com/forums/topic/263520-hsc02-round-3-muncher-pac-man-clone/


I think that many people will be surprised at just how good Muncher is on the Astrocade.

On July 7, 2006, I originally added the circa 1982 Astrocade Promotional video to BallyAlley.com.  The video's quality wasn't great, but it was the best that I could do at the time.  On May 9, 2012, Scott Stilphen took this video from BallyAlley and added it to YouTube.  I am glad that he did it, but I've always wanted a better version online.  This video was originally captured from a VHS tape in the Bob Fabris collection by Lance Squire.  He made a DVD of the Astrocade promotional video for me.  That DVD is the "original" source of the promotional video.

A few days ago, I made a much-higher quality version of the video.  This version looks much better, as it is from the DVD that Lance captured for me.  The video is now 1.11 GB (yes, it's quite large for just five minutes of footage).  I've just uploaded it to YouTube, but the YouTube video service has compressed the video quite a bit upon uploading, as now there are many examples of macroblocking and pixelation which aren't in my 1.11GB version of the video.  Even so, this newly uploaded version probably does look better than previously added versions of the promo video.

You can view the video here:


https://youtu.be/rLLMkv699Ac


I'm not sure how this video was originally distributed, as I don't think that this ever aired on TV in this full form.  In this video, a prototype version of Solar Conqueror is shown, not the released game.  Plus, Music Maker and Bowling (also both shown) were never officially released.

Today, I made a full transcription of the Astrocade Promotional video.  Here it is... Enjoy!  - Adam


If you took one of America's leading videogames and added three built-in games, four-player capability, a three-octave music synthesizer, 256 color variations, a built-in calculator, and a BASIC program (making it a personal home computer), you'd have Astrocade, The Professional Arcade, with a never-ending library of coin-op-quality exciting games.

Challenge the Incredible Wizard and his creatures in their treacherous dungeon. Slip through magic doors, outmaneuver the super monster, and if you shoot the Wizard, you'll experience the tremor of the entire dungeon as his magic wavers.

In Space Fortress, you command a lonely outpost, in a galaxy far, far away.  An alert sounds, and suddenly you're being attacked by alien ships in all directions.  You destroy some, but they keep coming, faster and faster.  It's positively addictive!

Galactic Invasion pits you against alien ships diving at your missile launcher from every direction.  They peel off from their formation (singly, or in teams or two or three).  The more aliens you destroy, the more their reinforcements attack.

Astrocade Pinball has everything but a slot to collect your quarters. Thumper bumpers, kicker targets, drop targets, even real flipper-action that catches the ball and rolls it back-and-forth so you can aim wherever you want.

There's no easier way to learn about computers than with the new Astrocade BASIC system. The plug-in cartridge, with built-in audio tape interface, converts your Astrocade into a personal computer that you can program yourself. The complete self-teaching instruction book will help you learn programming while you create electronic music, video art and computer games like these [shown on screen].

The following games are new releases from Astrocade's never ending library of home video games:

Solar Conqueror challenges you to dominate the galaxy. Conqueror solar systems while avoiding asteroids, and enemy spaceships that try to foil your efforts.  Speeding comets test your flying and shooting skills.  And the Space Warp shuttles you to new solar systems and more challenges.

Astrocade Bowling, it's like actually being at the alley. The game has all the action, sounds and excitement of the real thing. Direct your ball with as much hook as you want. Make strikes and spares, but watch out for splits and gutter balls. It can be played alone or by up to four players.  And scoring is kept according to official rules.

Music Maker lets you play your favorite songs and compose your own electric music. It has a three-octave range, plays three-note chords and has an automatic tempo setting. Music Maker sounds like a real organ and plays right through your own television speaker.  The musical notes are displayed on your TV screen. One hand control enters the music, and the computer automatically plays it back. Music Maker contains an audio cassette interface to allow you to record and store all of your musical arrangements.

Astrocade's Pirate's Chase, dares you to scoop up as many gold coins as you can carry.  But watch out; the pirates are on your trail!  How much of the treasure can you collect before Long John Silver collects you?

Artillery Duel will let you take your military positions, set your cannon and fire at your opposition. You'll even need to allow for wind and elevation while aiming and firing.

Cosmic Raiders takes you into deep space, where lies the alien sector, Larkin. Your mission: recover energy sources that have been seized by the evil Larkins. Radar and a superior guidance system will help you avoid the attacking kamikaze ships. The Energy Stars are near the Larkin Command Ship and you must retrieve them before you leave the sector.

This year, look forward to more excitement, more challenges and more fun with Astrocade, the home entertainment sensation.

Bob Fabris compiled these 21 examples of programs running on the Bally Arcade onto a 23-minute video in 1980.  The video is roughly edited (it would probably be considered fairly edited for its time).  It is shown here as Bob originally showed it at (I think) a computer show in 1980.  The video's pace is slow, but worth watching, as it shows what Bob believed to be top-notch (mostly) BASIC programs that would promote the Bally Arcade and his Arcadian newsletter (where many of these programs were first published)

This statement is at the end of the video, "All of this tape was produced using material provided by or to subscribers of the Arcadian, a newsletter devoted to the Bally machine and its uses. (C) Robert Fabris, 1980."

Hot Rod Bally BASIC is for use with a Bally Arcade/Astrocade equipped with expansion memory.  In this video, Jay Fenton narrates an insider's look at Hot Rod Bally BASIC.  He demonstrates eight, short expanded BASIC programs that make use of the extra features of the expanded BASIC, including extra colors that are available, and different sizes of fonts.

Vipersoft BASIC, also released on tape, is a slightly modified version of Hot Rod Bally BASIC that runs on a Viper RAM expansion.  There was a version of this expanded BASIC released on cartridge called Blue Ram BASIC that was for use with the Blue Ram expansion unit.

15117:
Lance Squire and I have exchanged a few emails back and forth about the Rotate routine written by Michael Matte.  Lance and I separately got a "cartridge" (ROM image) to work with the Astrocade emulator that uses the rotate function.  Lance noted that Michael's rotate routine doesn't seem to be compatible with the ROM WRITA subroutine.  I asked Michael some additional questions about his rotate function; he replied to me yesterday, saying:


"You asked 'Do you plan to extend the rotate function?' If you mean are you planning to provide any extended graphic routines utilizing the rotate function, I would say that's a good idea. Experimentation would be required to see if a pattern greater than 4 X 4 pixels can be rotated smoothly.

"The 'Write Absolute' subroutine (sub#38, WRITA) is a nonstandard write routine. It is not clear to me what the original intent of this subroutine call is and I'm wandering if access to it via the UPI was made available just because it is attached to subroutines 30, 32, 34 and 36. WRITA writes to screen RAM NOT to magic RAM and no output to the magic register (port OCH)  is even made. You can not 'OR' pixels, 'XOR' pixels, 'SHIFT' pixels, neither 'ROTATE' pixels with WRITA. I will mail you (via USPS) my handwritten detailed description on this 'Write Absolute' subroutine."


When I hear more from Michael, I'll post it here.

I myself am very close to tracking down the remaining Astrocade kiosks that were discarded by Montgomery Wards when they went out of business.  I was able to get in touch with the person who sold that kiosk to the person who then resold it on eBay several years back.  Turns out the Montgomery location they worked at had received an overstock of these kiosk that were meant to be distributed to the other stores and never got around to shipping them back to the main warehouse.   When their location closed down these were being disposed of and were pretty much up for grabs (which is how this person got a hold of one).  Apparently a lot of these old 'Wards employees still keep in touch with each other, and they have been a great help in tracking down and individual know as "Tom" who apparently took the bulk of the kiosk home in his pickup truck.  I was told by a reliable source that at a recent reunion of employees that Tom was still talking about them and still has a majority of them at his house.  Its just a matter of me getting a hold of him directly, as apparently Tom is a real old timer, doesn't have a computer, phone, etc.  I am hoping at their next reunion in June that the person I am in contact with can persuade Tom to correspond with me by mail (I have yet to get his address) and befriend him enough to let me take the trip to see him in person.  I am told he most likely has at least of dozen of them still in their original boxes.  Most likely if things fall into place I'll have to rent a u-hall and bring at least one other person to help me load them.  That, and a nice wad of cash I'm sure!  But a find like this would be priceless to myself and the community so I'm not worried about the cost.  Luckily my mother in law has finally gone semi-retired and is only working a few days a week, so I can use the money I'll save on day camp this summer and send the kids to stay with her instead.  She's always wanted to spend more time with them so this will be a win-win for both of us.  If anyone wants to volunteer when I go to pick these up let me know and I'll keep you in the loop on how things progress. 
-Michael  128Kgames.com 128K. Your Life Will Never Be The Same.

15138:
I'm scanning in letters from the Bob Fabris Collection. One letter caught my eye.  There are some great comments in a November 11, 1979 written to Bob Fabris from John Hurst.  I've OCRed the part of the letter that is interesting and have put it here.  Enjoy!  Any comments...?

Adam

The following are John Hurst's comments:

On Nov. 6, I received a phone call from Mr. Jack Nieman, Director of Sales, Bally Mfg. Co., in response to a letter that I had written on the 25th of Oct. It was the second letter I had sent since I never received an answer to my first one dated 4 Aug. The gist of the telephone conversation that I had with Mr. Nieman was as follows:
 
1.  Bally never advertised that there would be a keyboard add-on available.
 
2.  Bally is not happy with the amount of units purchased. (30,000)
 
3.  A DECISION will be made in January if the keyboard will be made.
 
4.  To make the keyboard feasible, 100,000 Arcade units would have to be sold, so that the percentage of keyboard sales would be high enough to warrant production.
 
5.  If the keyboard is not produced, the specifications, plans, and other info would be supplied to the ARCADIANS, for our use.
 
6.  Software for the Bally, except for the game cartridges, is not being produced because the retail price would be higher than what the ARCADIANS can get it from the newsletter, or club members selling it through the newsletter.
 
7.  Bally is still waiting for FCC specs, that will be needed if the Add-On is produced.
 
8.  Only 50% of the United States is being covered by Bally as far as distribution is concerned.
 
As you can see, there are no new answers, the same old ones, along with a lot of excuses. So, although I appreciated the phone call, I really didn't find out much useful new information.

15141:
Season 2, Round 4 of the Astrocade High Score Club has begun.  It will last about three weeks. This round ends on Sunday, April 30'th at 8pm MST.  The main game is Sneaky Snake.  The BASIC bonus game is Caterpillar.


Sneaky Snake is a 4K machine language cartridge released by New Image.  It was programmed on the Astrocade by Dave Ibach and assembled using the General Video Assembler.  This game tried to be true to the original arcade game by keeping Centipede's original vertical monitor setup.


The BASIC bonus game is 1983's type-in game Caterpillar, by Thadd*Pro (Kevin O'Neill).  This appeared in two newsletters.  It is an "AstroBASIC" variant on the classic videogame, Snake.  In this case, you move a caterpillar around the screen, growing ever longer while you pick up items for points.  Unlike other versions of Snake, you grow continuously, not only when you eat snacks.  In my eyes, Caterpillar mixes Checkmate with Snake and comes up with an interesting variant.

You can read the full details about round 4, here:


http://atariage.com/forums/topic/264390-hsc02-round-4-sneaky-snake-caterpillar/


Remember, please post all scores in the AtariAge forums, as scores submitted here are not accepted.


Come join us Astro-Bugs over at AtariAge!  If you don't, then I'm gonna keep buggin' you!

Adam
